questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT a keyword in C?
questions.explanation_en: volatile, sizeof and register are all reserved C keywords (sizeof is a keyword that works as an operator). include is not a keyword; #include is a preprocessor directive handled before compilation.

questions.chapter: Programming — Programming Basics: Data Types, Operators & Control Flow
questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT a reserved keyword in Java?
questions.explanation_en: true, false and null are literals, not keywords, although they still cannot be used as identifiers. goto and const are reserved keywords that Java does not use, and strictfp is a keyword for floating-point behaviour.

questions.chapter: Programming — Programming Basics: Data Types, Operators & Control Flow
questions.explanation_en: When an int and an unsigned int are compared, the usual arithmetic conversions turn the int into unsigned int. -1 becomes the largest unsigned value, 4294967295 with a 32-bit int. 4294967295 < 1 is false, so the else part prints greater.

questions.chapter: Programming — Programming Basics: Data Types, Operators & Control Flow
questions.explanation_en: sizeof(c) is the size of a char variable, which is always 1. In C a character constant such as 'A' has type int, not char, so sizeof('A') equals sizeof(int), which is 4. (In C++ a character literal is a char, so it would print 1 1.)

questions.chapter: Programming — Programming Basics: Data Types, Operators & Control Flow
questions.question_en: Which of the following Java declarations compiles without error?
questions.explanation_en: An int constant can be assigned to a char, byte or short if its value fits, and 65 fits in char (it is 'A'). 3.5 is a double literal, so float needs 3.5f. 9999999999 is too big for an int literal and needs the L suffix. 128 is outside the byte range -128 to 127.

questions.chapter: Programming — Programming Basics: Data Types, Operators & Control Flow
questions.question_en: Which of the following is a valid identifier in C?
questions.explanation_en: An identifier may contain letters, digits and underscores, but must not start with a digit and must not be a keyword. _total2 follows these rules. 2total starts with a digit, total-2 contains a minus sign, and int is a keyword.

questions.chapter: Programming — Programming Basics: Data Types, Operators & Control Flow
questions.question_en: What is the default storage class of a local variable declared inside a function in C?
questions.explanation_en: Local variables are auto by default: they are created when the block is entered, destroyed when it ends, and hold garbage if not initialised. The auto keyword is therefore rarely written. static, extern and register must be written explicitly.

C passes arguments by value, so a and b are copies of x and y. swap() exchanges only its own copies, which are destroyed when it returns. x and y in main() are unchanged, so 3 9 is printed. To swap them you must pass pointers (&x, &y).
Arguments fill parameters from the left, and missing trailing ones take their defaults. vol(4) = 4*2*3 = 24. vol(4, 5) sets b = 5 and keeps h = 3, so 4*5*3 = 60. vol(1, 2, 7) = 1*2*7 = 14.

questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python 3 code?
```python
def g(s):
    if len(s) <= 1:
        return s
    return g(s[1:]) + s[0]

print(g("exam"))
```
questions.explanation_en: Each call moves the first character to the end of the reversed rest. g("exam") = g("xam") + "e" = (g("am") + "x") + "e" = ((g("m") + "a") + "x") + "e". g("m") returns "m", so the result is "maxe", the reversed string.
m() is Euclid's GCD algorithm. m(84, 36) calls m(36, 84 % 36) = m(36, 12), which calls m(12, 36 % 12) = m(12, 0). Since b is 0, it returns 12, the greatest common divisor of 84 and 36.

questions.question_en: In C++, two functions with the same name CANNOT be overloaded if they differ only in their
questions.explanation_en: The compiler chooses an overload from the arguments in the call, and a call does not show which return type is wanted. So functions that differ only in return type cause a redeclaration error. They must differ in the number, types or order of their parameters.
r is a reference, another name for a, so r += v changes a to 4 + 6 = 10. v is passed by value, so v *= 2 changes only the local copy and b stays 6. Output: 10 6.

Java always passes by value; for an array the value passed is a copy of the reference. arr[0] = 99 changes the caller's array through that copy. n = 99 changes only the local int. After arr is pointed at a new array, arr[1] = 77 changes the new array, not a. So a is {99, 2} and n is 1.

questions.question_en: In C++, declaring a function with the inline keyword

options.en: forces the compiler to expand every call
is only a request; the compiler may ignore it
makes the function run in a separate thread
is allowed only for recursive functions

questions.explanation_en: inline asks the compiler to replace each call with the function body, which saves call overhead for small functions. It is only a request: the compiler may refuse, for example for large, recursive or complex functions. It has nothing to do with threads.

questions.question_en: Which of the following C++ function declarations is INVALID?

options.en: int f(int a, int b = 1, int c = 2);
int f(int a = 1, int b, int c = 2);
int f(int a, int b, int c = 2);
int f(int a = 0, int b = 1, int c = 2);

questions.explanation_en: Default arguments must be given from right to left: once a parameter has a default, every parameter after it must also have one. In int f(int a = 1, int b, int c = 2) the parameter b has no default although a, before it, has one, so the declaration is an error.

questions.question_en: In a C variadic function, which macro from <stdarg.h> is used to fetch the next unnamed argument?
questions.explanation_en: va_list is the type of the argument pointer. va_start(ap, last) initialises it after the last named parameter, va_arg(ap, type) returns the next argument as the given type, and va_end(ap) cleans up. Only va_arg actually fetches an argument.
The first argument n = 3 tells sum() how many values to read. The loop calls va_arg three times and adds 10 + 20 + 30 = 60. The extra argument 40 is passed but never read, which is allowed.

A static local is initialised only once and keeps its value between calls; an ordinary local is re-created each call. First call: s = 2, a = 2, returns 22. Second call: s = 3 but a starts again at 1 and becomes 2, so it returns 32.

An inner declaration hides an outer one only inside its own block. The inner block sees its own x = 30. After the block ends, main() sees its local x = 20. show() cannot see main()'s locals, so it uses the global x = 10.

Each call prints n before the recursive call and again after it returns. Going down, p(3), p(2), p(1) print 3, 2, 1; p(0) prints nothing and returns. Unwinding, p(1), p(2), p(3) print 1, 2, 3. Output: 321123.

Let C(n) be the number of calls for fib(n): C(0) = C(1) = 1 and C(n) = 1 + C(n-1) + C(n-2). So C(2) = 3, C(3) = 5, C(4) = 9 and C(5) = 1 + 9 + 5 = 15. The program prints fib(5) = 5, but fib() is called 15 times.

questions.question_en: Compared with an equivalent iterative (loop) solution, a recursive function usually

options.en: runs faster, because no loop is needed
uses more memory, as every call adds a stack frame
cannot return a value to its caller

questions.explanation_en: Every recursive call pushes a new stack frame holding its parameters, locals and return address, so recursion needs more memory and has call overhead. Too deep a recursion can overflow the stack. Recursion can return values, and it always needs a base case to stop.

questions.question_en: A recursive function whose recursive call is the very last operation it performs is said to use
questions.explanation_en: In tail recursion nothing is left to do after the recursive call returns, so compilers can reuse the same stack frame (tail-call optimisation). Head recursion makes the call first and works afterwards, indirect recursion is A calling B calling A, and nested recursion passes a recursive call as an argument.

questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python 3 code?
```python
def add(x, lst=[]):
    lst.append(x)
    return lst

add(1)
add(2)
print(add(3))
```
questions.explanation_en: A default value is evaluated only once, when the def statement runs, so all three calls share the same list object. add(1) makes it [1], add(2) makes it [1, 2], and add(3) makes it [1, 2, 3], which is printed. The usual fix is lst=None and creating a new list inside.

f(95) = f(f(106)) = f(96), because f(106) = 96. In the same way f(96) = f(97) = f(98) = f(99) = f(100). Then f(100) = f(f(111)) = f(101) = 91. This is McCarthy's 91 function: it returns 91 for any n <= 100.

Java resolves overloads in phases: first without boxing or varargs, then with boxing, then with varargs. For m(5) the first phase already finds m(long) by widening int to long, so long is printed. For m(Integer.valueOf(5)) the argument is already an Integer, so m(Integer) matches exactly.
When an array has an initialiser list shorter than its size, the listed values go to the first elements and every remaining element is set to 0. So a = {3, 7, 0, 0, 0}, a[1] = 7 and a[4] = 0.

questions.question_en: A 2-D array int A[10][20] is stored in row-major order starting at address 2000, and each int takes 4 bytes. What is the address of A[3][5] (indices start at 0)?
questions.explanation_en: In row-major order, Address = Base + (i * columns + j) * size. Here that is 2000 + (3 * 20 + 5) * 4 = 2000 + 65 * 4 = 2260. 2212 is the column-major answer, (5 * 10 + 3) * 4 + 2000.

questions.question_en: An array B[1..10][1..15] (10 rows, 15 columns) is stored in column-major order. The base address is 500 and each element takes 2 bytes. What is the address of B[4][6]?
questions.explanation_en: In column-major order with lower bounds 1, Address = Base + ((j - 1) * rows + (i - 1)) * size. That is 500 + ((6 - 1) * 10 + (4 - 1)) * 2 = 500 + 53 * 2 = 606. 600 is the row-major result, 500 + (3 * 15 + 5) * 2.
The array size is taken from the 6 initialisers. sizeof(a) is the whole array, 6 * 4 = 24 bytes, and sizeof(a[0]) is one int, 4 bytes. 24 / 4 = 6, the number of elements.

questions.question_en: In C, an int pointer p holds the address 1000. If sizeof(int) is 4, what address does p + 3 hold?
questions.explanation_en: Adding n to a pointer moves it by n elements, not n bytes. For an int pointer each step is sizeof(int) = 4 bytes, so p + 3 = 1000 + 3 * 4 = 1012.

questions.question_en: In C, an array int a[10] is passed to a function declared as void f(int arr[]). What does sizeof(arr) give inside f()?

options.en: 40, the size of the whole array
The size of an int pointer, not of the array

questions.explanation_en: An array argument decays to a pointer to its first element, and a parameter written as int arr[] is really int *arr. So sizeof(arr) inside f() is the size of a pointer (4 or 8 bytes), not 10 * sizeof(int). That is why the length is usually passed as a separate argument.

questions.question_en: Which C header file declares the functions strlen(), strcpy() and strcmp()?
questions.explanation_en: The string-handling functions such as strlen(), strcpy(), strcat(), strcmp() and strchr() are declared in <string.h>. ctype.h holds character tests like isdigit() and toupper(), and stdlib.h holds malloc(), atoi() and similar.

questions.question_en: What is the main difference between malloc() and calloc() in C?

options.en: malloc() sets the allocated bytes to zero; calloc() does not
calloc() allocates on the stack; malloc() on the heap
Only memory from malloc() has to be released with free()
calloc() sets the allocated bytes to zero; malloc() does not

questions.explanation_en: Both allocate memory on the heap and both blocks must be released with free(). calloc(n, size) allocates n * size bytes and fills them with zero. malloc(size) leaves the contents uninitialised (garbage).

questions.question_en: What does malloc() return in C when the requested memory cannot be allocated?
questions.explanation_en: malloc(), calloc() and realloc() return NULL when they cannot allocate the requested block. A program should therefore check the returned pointer against NULL before using it.

questions.question_en: Given int a[5]; int *p = a; in C, which of the following statements is INVALID?
questions.explanation_en: An array name stands for the fixed address of its first element and is not a modifiable lvalue, so a++ (or a = p) is a compilation error. p is an ordinary pointer variable, so p++ is fine. *(a + 1) = 3 and a[0] = a[1] only change elements, which is allowed.

questions.question_en: In C, what does the declaration int *const p = &x; mean?

options.en: *p cannot be changed, but p can point elsewhere
p cannot be changed, but *p (the value of x) can
Neither p nor *p can be changed
p is a pointer to a constant integer

questions.explanation_en: Read the declaration from right to left: p is a const pointer to int. The pointer itself is fixed and must stay pointing at x, but *p = 5 is allowed. const int *p (pointer to const int) is the opposite: p can move but *p cannot be changed through it.

questions.question_en: In C, the statements char *s = "hello"; s[0] = 'H'; result in

options.en: undefined behaviour, as a string literal must not be modified
s holding Hello on every compiler and system
a compilation error on every C compiler
s pointing to a fresh, writable copy of the string

questions.explanation_en: s points to a string literal, which may be stored in read-only memory; trying to change it is undefined behaviour (often a crash). It still compiles, because in C a literal has type char[]. To get a modifiable string use an array: char s[] = "hello";
strcat(a, b) appends b to the end of a, so a becomes "Teacher" (a[20] has room for it). strlen() counts characters up to, but not including, the terminating '\0', so it returns 7.
Java always initialises array elements to default values. Numeric types get 0 (0.0 for double), boolean gets false, and reference types such as String get null. So the line prints 0 null false 0.0.
A Java 2-D array is an array of row arrays, and rows can have different lengths. m.length is the number of rows, 3. m[2] is {5, 6}, so m[2].length is 2, and m[1][0] is 4.
p points to a[1]. *(p + 2) is a[3] = 40, and p[-1] means *(p - 1), which is a[0] = 10. In *p + 2 the * binds first, so it is a[1] + 2 = 22, not *(p + 2).
a[i] is defined as *(a + i), and since addition is commutative, 2[a] = *(2 + a) = a[2] = 6. *(a + 1) is a[1] = 4 and a[3] = 8. Multiplication comes first: 6 + 4 * 8 = 38.
q points to p and p points to x, so **q and *p both mean x. **q = **q * 3 makes x = 21, and *p += 1 makes x = 22. **q == *p compares x with x, which is true, so it prints 1.
p and q both point to m. *q = *p + 4 stores 6 + 4 = 10 into m. Then *p * m / 5 = 10 * 10 / 5 = 100 / 5 = 20 (the first * is dereference, the second is multiplication).

strlen() counts characters before '\0', so it is 5 for "Delhi". sizeof gives the size of the whole array: s was declared with 20 elements, so 20. t's size comes from the initialiser, 5 letters plus '\0', so 6.

new int[4]{2, 4, 6, 8} allocates and initialises a dynamic array. q starts at p and moves 2 elements at a time, so it visits p[0] = 2 and p[2] = 6; at p + 4 the loop stops. s = 2 + 6 = 8, and delete[] frees the array.

All members of a union share the same memory, so its size is the size of the largest member, rounded up for alignment. The largest member is double (8 bytes); c[6] needs only 6. So sizeof(union U) is 8, whereas a struct with the same members would need at least 18.

== compares references, equals() compares contents. "ja" + "va" is a compile-time constant, so b refers to the same pooled literal as a, and a == b is true. new String() always creates a new object, so a == c is false, but a.equals(c) is true.

Java String objects are immutable. toUpperCase() and concat() return new String objects, but the results are thrown away because they are not assigned to anything. s still refers to "abc", so the output is abc followed by its length 3.
*(m + 1) is the row m[1], and adding 2 moves to its element at index 2, so *(*(m + 1) + 2) = m[1][2] = 7. m[2] + 3 points to m[2][3], so the second value is 12.

The loop moves p along the string until it reaches the terminating '\0' (the condition *p becomes 0). For each digit character, *p - '0' converts it to its numeric value. The digits are 1, 2 and 3, so n = 6. Adding the ASCII codes instead (49 + 50 + 51) would give 150.

*p++ means *(p++): it reads a[0] = 5 into x and then moves p to a[1]. (*p)++ reads a[1] = 10 into y and then increments a[1] to 11. ++*p increments a[1] again to 12 and gives 12 to z. So x = 5, y = 10, z = 12 and a[1] = 12.
The literal holds a, b, '\0', c, d plus the automatic terminating '\0', so the array has 6 bytes and sizeof(s) is 6. strlen() stops at the first '\0', which comes right after "ab", so it returns 2.

c takes byte 0, then 3 padding bytes are added so that i starts at offset 4 (bytes 4 to 7). d takes byte 8. The total is then padded up to a multiple of 4, the struct's alignment, giving 12. Simply adding the members (1 + 4 + 1) would give 6.

A string literal is a char array, so n + "Delhi%d" is a pointer 3 characters past its start. D, e and l are skipped, and the format string printf() receives is "hi%d". The %d is replaced by n, so the output is hi3.

questions.question_en: Which OOP feature is summed up by the phrase "one interface, many forms"?
questions.explanation_en: Polymorphism (Greek: many forms) lets one name or interface stand for different behaviours, for example one method name with several implementations. Encapsulation bundles data with methods, and inheritance lets a class reuse another class's members.

Every constructor first calls its superclass constructor (an implicit super() call). new C() calls B(), which calls A(). A() prints A, then control returns and B() prints B, then C() prints C. Output: ABC.

questions.question_en: Binding data and the methods that work on that data into a single unit (a class) is called:
questions.explanation_en: Encapsulation wraps data members and member functions together in a class and usually hides the data behind private access. This protects the data from direct outside access.

Creating d runs the base constructor first (B), then the derived constructor (D). When d goes out of scope at the end of main, destructors run in the reverse order: ~Derived prints ~D, then ~Base prints ~B. Output: B D ~D ~B.

Overloading is resolved at compile time by choosing the most specific method. byte has no exact match, so it widens to int, the closest type: int. 5L is a long: long. 5.0f is a float with no float version, so it widens to double: double. Output: int long double.

questions.question_en: Which of the following operators CANNOT be overloaded in C++?
questions.explanation_en: C++ does not allow overloading of :: (scope resolution), . (member access), .* (pointer-to-member), ?: (conditional) and sizeof. Operators such as +, [] and << can be overloaded; << is commonly overloaded for output with cout.
The reference a has type Animal but points to a Dog object. Java instance methods are bound at run time (dynamic method dispatch), so the overriding Dog.sound() runs. Output: Bark.

questions.question_en: Which statement about a friend function of a class in C++ is TRUE?

options.en: It is not a member but can access the class's private members
It is a member function that can access only public members
It is automatically inherited by all derived classes
It must be called through an object using the dot operator

questions.explanation_en: A friend function is declared inside the class with the keyword friend but is not a member of the class. It can still access the class's private and protected members. It is called like an ordinary function, and friendship is not inherited.

Only instance methods are overridden and chosen at run time. Fields and static methods are chosen by the reference type at compile time. The reference type is P, so obj.x is 10 and obj.s() is "P"; obj.m() runs Q's version and gives "Q". 10 + "P" + "Q" = "10PQ".

questions.question_en: Method overloading in Java is an example of:
questions.explanation_en: In overloading, methods share a name but differ in their parameter lists, and the compiler picks the version from the argument types. That is compile-time polymorphism. Overriding is resolved at run time (dynamic method dispatch).

p is a Shape* pointing to a Circle. name() is not virtual, so the call is bound at compile time by the pointer type: Shape::name() prints Shape. area() is virtual, so the call is bound at run time by the object type: Circle::area() prints CircleArea. Output: Shape CircleArea.

questions.question_en: Which statement about Java interfaces (Java 8 and later) is TRUE?

options.en: An interface can have non-final instance variables
An interface can declare a public constructor
An interface can have default and static methods with a body
A class can implement only one interface at a time

questions.explanation_en: Since Java 8 an interface may contain default and static methods with bodies (and private methods since Java 9). Interface fields are always public static final, interfaces have no constructors, and a class may implement many interfaces.

count is static, so all objects share one copy. id is an instance variable, so each object has its own copy. a: count=1, id=1; b: count=2, id=2; c: count=3, id=3. Printing a.id, b.id and Counter.count gives 1 2 3.

questions.question_en: Which statement about the final keyword in Java is FALSE?

options.en: A final method can be overridden in a subclass
A final class cannot be extended by another class
A final variable can be assigned a value only once
A blank final variable can be assigned in the constructor

questions.explanation_en: A final method cannot be overridden, so that statement is false. A final class cannot be subclassed (for example String), and a final variable gets its value exactly once. A blank final instance variable can be given its value in a constructor.

this(...) must be the first statement, so each constructor calls the next before printing. Box() calls Box(5), which calls Box(5, 5). Box(5, 5) sets w = h = 5 and prints WH; control then returns to print S, then D. b.w * b.h = 25, so the output is WHSD 25.

questions.question_en: Arrange the Java access levels from MOST restrictive to LEAST restrictive.
questions.explanation_en: private allows access only inside the class. Default (package-private, no keyword) adds the same package. protected adds subclasses in other packages. public allows access from everywhere. So the order is private > default > protected > public.

The object is a SportsCar, so SportsCar.type() runs. It returns "Sports-" + super.type(), where super refers to Car. Car.type() returns "Car-" + Vehicle.type(), which is "Car-Vehicle". Result: Sports-Car-Vehicle.

questions.question_en: In C++, which access specifier makes a base-class member accessible in its derived classes but not to unrelated outside code?
questions.explanation_en: A protected member can be used inside the class and inside classes derived from it, but not by unrelated code. A private member is not accessible even in derived classes, and a public member is accessible everywhere. virtual is not an access specifier.

Autoboxing uses Integer.valueOf(), which returns cached objects for values from -128 to 127. a and b refer to the same cached object, so a == b is true. 200 is outside the cache, so c and d are different objects and c == d is false. equals() compares the values: true.

questions.question_en: Which type of inheritance is NOT supported in Java through classes?
questions.explanation_en: A Java class can extend only one class, so multiple inheritance of classes is not allowed. This avoids the diamond problem. A class can still implement several interfaces, which gives multiple inheritance of type.

A static block runs once, when the class is loaded, before the first object is created: S. For every object, the instance initializer block runs before the constructor body: I then C. Two objects give S + IC + IC = SICIC.

questions.question_en: Which statement correctly describes how the JDK, JRE and JVM are related?

options.en: The JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM
The JVM contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JDK
The JRE contains the JDK, and the JDK contains the JVM
The JDK and the JRE do not use the JVM at all

questions.explanation_en: The JVM executes bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the core class libraries needed to run programs. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, javadoc and jar. So JDK > JRE > JVM.

An abstract class cannot be instantiated, but it can have a constructor, which runs when a subclass object is created. new Square(3) first runs Shape() (prints Shape), then the Square body (prints Square). area() returns the double 3.0 * 3.0, which prints as 9.0.

questions.question_en: The Java compiler (javac) translates a .java source file into:

options.en: Native machine code in an .exe file

questions.explanation_en: javac produces platform-independent bytecode in .class files. The JVM on any platform then interprets this bytecode or JIT-compiles it. This is the basis of "write once, run anywhere".

null can be passed to both versions. Java then chooses the most specific method, and String is more specific than Object because String is a subclass of Object. So f(String) is called and prints String. There is no ambiguity, so the code compiles.

questions.question_en: In the Java ClassLoader delegation hierarchy, which class loader has NO parent class loader?
questions.explanation_en: The Bootstrap (primordial) ClassLoader is written in native code and loads the core Java classes. It is the root of the hierarchy, so it has no parent. Its child is the Platform/Extension loader, whose child is the Application/System loader, which has no child loaders by default.

Hindi overrides the default method greet(). Inside the override, Greeter.super.greet() calls the interface's default version, which returns "Hello". The call g.greet() runs Hindi's version at run time and returns "Namaste Hello".

questions.question_en: Which statement about Java packages is TRUE?

options.en: Each package can contain only a single class or interface
An import statement copies the class code into the file
The java.lang package must always be imported explicitly
They prevent naming conflicts and provide controlled access

questions.explanation_en: A package groups related classes, so two classes with the same name can live in different packages, and default/protected access is controlled at package level. import only lets you use short names; it copies no code. java.lang is imported automatically.

n is static, so one copy is shared by all objects; it starts at 0. Creating a and b calls the constructor twice (n = 2). The array c[3] creates three more objects, and the constructor runs for each one (n = 5). Output: 5.

questions.question_en: In C++, what does the statement cin.ignore(100, '\n'); do?

options.en: Discards the last 100 characters typed before the '\n' character
Discards up to 100 input characters, stopping once '\n' is discarded
Reads 100 characters into a buffer, skipping only the '\n' character
Waits 100 milliseconds for the user to press the Enter key

questions.explanation_en: istream::ignore(n, delim) extracts and throws away characters from the input stream. It stops after n characters or after the delimiter has been extracted, whichever comes first. It is often used to remove the leftover newline from the buffer.

T a; calls the default constructor: D. T b = a; makes a new object from an existing one, so the copy constructor runs: C. f(a) passes the object by value, so the parameter x is made with the copy constructor: C. Output: DCC.

questions.question_en: In a C++ program, the statement cin >> age; is followed by getline(cin, name);, and name gets an empty string. Why?

options.en: getline cannot read any string that contains blank spaces
getline reads the newline that cin >> left in the input buffer
cin >> always clears the whole input buffer after reading
getline reads only from files and never from the keyboard

questions.explanation_en: cin >> age reads the number but leaves the Enter key's '\n' in the buffer. getline reads up to the next '\n', finds it at once, and returns an empty string. Calling cin.ignore() before getline removes the leftover newline.

add(2, 3) has int arguments, so the int version runs and returns 2 + 3 = 5. add(2.0, 3.0) has double arguments, so the double version runs and returns 2.0 * 3.0 = 6.0. cout prints the double 6.0 as 6 by default. Output: 5 6.

questions.question_en: In C++, a class becomes an abstract class when it:

options.en: Declares at least one pure virtual function (= 0)
Has no data members of its own
Is declared with the keyword abstract

questions.explanation_en: A pure virtual function is declared like virtual void draw() = 0;. A class with at least one such function is abstract and cannot be instantiated. C++ has no abstract keyword; that keyword belongs to Java and C#.

final makes the reference arr constant: it cannot point to another array. The elements can still be changed, so arr[0] = 10 is legal. arr[0] + arr.length is int + int = 10 + 3 = 13 (numeric addition, not string joining).
The return 1 in try is prepared first, but the finally block always runs before the method actually returns. So F is printed inside f(), and only then does main() receive 1 and print it, giving F 1.
When return x executes, the value 20 is saved as the return value. finally then runs and sets the local variable x to 30, but that does not change the value already saved. The method returns 20.

The exception is caught and the catch block prepares to return 2. The finally block always runs afterwards, and its own return 3 replaces the pending return value. So h() returns 3. (A return in finally is legal but bad practice, as it can hide exceptions.)

a has indexes 0 and 1, so a[2] = 5 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and A is skipped. Only the first matching catch runs, printing B. finally then prints D, and since the exception was handled, the program continues and prints E.

ArithmeticException is a subclass of Exception, so any ArithmeticException is already caught by the first block. The compiler reports the second catch as unreachable ("exception has already been caught"). More specific exceptions must be caught before more general ones.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is a checked exception in Java?
questions.explanation_en: Checked exceptions are subclasses of Exception that are not subclasses of RuntimeException; the compiler forces you to catch or declare them. IOException is checked. NullPointerException, ArithmeticException and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException extend RuntimeException, so they are unchecked.

questions.question_en: In Java, which class is the direct superclass of both Exception and Error?
questions.explanation_en: java.lang.Throwable is the root of everything that can be thrown or caught; it has two direct subclasses, Exception and Error. RuntimeException and IOException are subclasses of Exception, and Thread is unrelated.

questions.question_en: In Java, the throws keyword is used to

options.en: declare in a method header the exceptions it may pass to its caller
throw an exception object explicitly from inside a block
catch every exception raised inside the method body
run clean-up code whether or not an exception occurs

questions.explanation_en: throws appears in a method declaration, for example void read() throws IOException, and tells callers which checked exceptions they must handle. throw (without s) is the statement that actually throws an exception object. Catching is done by catch, and clean-up by finally.

"1 " is printed, then throw 5 throws an int and the rest of the try block is skipped. Catch handlers are matched by type without the usual int-to-double conversion, so catch (double) is skipped and catch (int) receives 5. Output: 1 I5.

questions.question_en: In C++, if a thrown exception is not caught by any handler, which function is called automatically?
questions.explanation_en: When no matching catch is found, the C++ runtime calls std::terminate(), which by default calls std::abort() and ends the program abnormally. exit() and atexit() are for normal termination, and rethrow_exception() rethrows a stored exception.

questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python 3 code?

def test(x):
    try:
        r = 10 // x
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("Z", end=" ")
    else:
        print("E", end=" ")
    finally:
        print("F", end=" ")

test(2)
test(0)
```

questions.question_en: In Python 3, which exception is raised by the statement import xyzlib when no module named xyzlib is installed?
questions.explanation_en: When Python cannot find a module to import, it raises ModuleNotFoundError, which is a subclass of ImportError (so except ImportError also catches it). NameError is for an undefined name, FileNotFoundError for a missing file in open(), and AttributeError for a missing attribute.

questions.question_en: In Java, an ordinary try block (not try-with-resources) must be followed by

options.en: at least one catch block, a finally block, or both
exactly one catch block and exactly one finally block
a throws clause on the enclosing method

questions.explanation_en: A plain try must have at least one catch or a finally (or both); a try alone is a compilation error. It may have many catch blocks but at most one finally. A throws clause is optional and unrelated to this rule.

questions.question_en: In Java, in which of the following situations does the finally block NOT execute?

options.en: The try block executes a return statement
An exception is caught by a catch block
No exception is thrown in the try block
System.exit(0) is called inside the try block

questions.explanation_en: finally runs after normal completion, after a caught or uncaught exception, and even after return, break or continue. The main exception is System.exit(), which stops the JVM at once, so the finally block never runs (a JVM crash or power failure has the same effect).

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas

What is the output of the following Python code?

print(max("Delhi"), min("Delhi"))

questions.explanation_en: max() and min() on a string compare Unicode (ASCII) values. D=68, e=101, l=108, h=104, i=105. The largest is 'l' (108). The smallest is the capital 'D' (68), because uppercase letters have smaller codes than lowercase ones.

questions.explanation_en: strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace, giving "Delhi", so the first part prints [Delhi]. rstrip() removes only the trailing spaces, giving "  Delhi": 2 spaces + 5 letters = 7 characters.

print("a,b,,c".split(","), len("a b  c".split()))

questions.explanation_en: With an explicit separator, split(",") cuts at every comma, so the two commas side by side give an empty string: ['a', 'b', '', 'c']. With no argument, split() splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty pieces, so "a b  c" gives ['a', 'b', 'c'], of length 3.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: For a Python string s, what happens when the substring is NOT found by s.find(sub) and by s.index(sub)?

options.en: Both return -1 when sub is not found
Both return None when sub is not found

questions.explanation_en: Both methods return the lowest index where sub starts. They differ only when sub is absent: find() returns -1, while index() raises ValueError: substring not found.

L.append([3, 4])
L.extend([5, 6])
print(len(L), L)

questions.explanation_en: append() adds its argument as one element, so the whole list [3, 4] becomes one item: [1, 2, [3, 4]]. extend() adds each element of the iterable separately: [1, 2, [3, 4], 5, 6]. That is 5 elements.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas

L = [3, 1, 2]
x = L.sort()
print(x, L)

questions.explanation_en: list.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None, like append(), extend(), insert(), remove() and reverse(). So x is None, and L itself is now [1, 2, 3]. Use sorted(L) when a new sorted list is wanted.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = a[:]
b.append(4)
c.append(5)
print(a, len(c))

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas

L = [10, 20, 30, 40]

L.pop()

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas

t[1].append(4)
print(t, len(t))

questions.question_en: Which pair of methods is available on a Python tuple object?
questions.explanation_en: A tuple is immutable, so it has only the two methods that do not change it: count(x) and index(x). append, extend, sort and reverse are list methods, and add/remove are set methods (list also has remove).

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
s = {3, 1, 3, 2, 1}
s.add(2)
s.add(4)
print(len(s), sorted(s))
```
questions.explanation_en: A set keeps only unique elements, so {3, 1, 3, 2, 1} is {1, 2, 3}. add(2) changes nothing because 2 is already there; add(4) adds 4. The set has 4 elements, and sorted() returns them as a sorted list: [1, 2, 3, 4].

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: Which of the following CANNOT be used as a key in a Python dictionary?
questions.explanation_en: Dictionary keys must be hashable, which in practice means immutable. Strings, numbers and tuples of immutable items can be keys. A list is mutable and unhashable, so {[1, 2]: 'x'} raises TypeError. Values can be of any type.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
d = {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'a': 3}
print(d, len(d))
```
questions.explanation_en: Keys are unique. When a key is repeated, the later value replaces the earlier one, but the key keeps its first position. So 'a' stays first with value 3, and the dictionary has 2 items.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
d = {'x': 10}
print(d.get('y'), d.get('y', 0), d.setdefault('z', 5), len(d))
```
questions.explanation_en: get('y') returns None for a missing key instead of raising KeyError. get('y', 0) returns the default 0, and neither call adds a key. setdefault('z', 5) inserts 'z': 5 because 'z' is missing and returns 5. d now has 2 keys.

questions.question_en: In Python 3.7 and later, what does d.popitem() remove from a dictionary d?

options.en: The pair with the smallest key

questions.explanation_en: From Python 3.7, dictionaries keep insertion order, and popitem() removes and returns the most recently inserted (key, value) pair (LIFO order). It raises KeyError if the dictionary is empty. pop(key) removes a chosen key.

questions.explanation_en: A loop's else block runs only if the loop ends without break. The for loop counts 3 and 7 (count = 2), then breaks at 10, so its else is skipped and count stays 2. The while loop ends normally when i becomes 3, so its else runs and i = 30.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
def f(a, b=2, c=3):
    return a + b * c
print(f(1), f(1, c=1), f(1, 4))
```
questions.explanation_en: f(1): a=1, b=2, c=3, so 1 + 2*3 = 7. f(1, c=1): b keeps its default 2, so 1 + 2*1 = 3. f(1, 4): the second positional argument sets b=4 and c=3, so 1 + 4*3 = 13.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items
add(1)
print(add(2), add(3, []))
```
questions.explanation_en: A default value is created once, when def runs, and is shared by all calls that use it. add(1) makes the default list [1]; add(2) uses the same list, giving [1, 2]. add(3, []) is given a new empty list, so it returns [3].

questions.question_en: The statement import pandas stops with ModuleNotFoundError, a subclass of ImportError. What does this mean?

options.en: The pandas module was found but contains a syntax error
pandas was imported successfully but is an old version
The program file was not saved with a .py extension
Python could not find the pandas module in its search path

questions.explanation_en: ImportError (and its subclass ModuleNotFoundError) is raised when Python cannot find or load the module named in an import statement. The usual cause is that the library is not installed in the current environment, which pip install pandas fixes.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: After the statement import math as m, which of the following calls works?
questions.explanation_en: import math as m binds the module only to the name m, so its functions are used as m.sqrt(25), which gives 5.0. The name math is not defined, and sqrt alone would need from math import sqrt.

questions.question_en: Which file mode opens a file for both reading and appending, creates the file if it does not exist, and sends every write to the end of the file?
questions.explanation_en: a+ opens for appending and reading, creates a missing file, and always writes at the end, keeping the old data. r+ is read/write with the pointer at the start and needs an existing file. w+ is write/read but empties the file first. rb is read-only binary.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: Which file mode opens a file for writing and reading but first erases any existing contents?
questions.explanation_en: w and w+ truncate an existing file to zero length, or create it if it is missing. w+ also allows reading. r+ keeps the contents and starts at the beginning, a+ keeps the contents and writes at the end, and rb only reads in binary.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: Which of the following modes raises FileNotFoundError when the file does not already exist?
questions.explanation_en: The read modes (r, r+, rb, rb+) need an existing file and raise FileNotFoundError otherwise. The modes w, w+, a and a+ create the file if it is missing.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: Which of the following is normally handled as a binary file (opened with a mode such as 'rb') in Python?
questions.explanation_en: Text files (.txt, .csv, .py, .html) hold readable characters stored line by line and are opened in text mode. Images, audio, video and .exe files hold raw bytes that are not text, so they are opened in binary mode ('rb', 'wb'), and read() returns bytes.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("one\ntwo\nthree\n")
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    a = f.readline()
    b = f.read(3)
    c = f.readlines()
print(repr(a), b, len(c))
```
questions.explanation_en:
readline() reads one line including its newline, so a is 'one
'. read(3) reads the next 3 characters: two. The pointer is now just before the newline after two, so readlines() returns ['
', 'three
'], a list of length 2.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
with open("s.txt", "w") as f:
    n = f.write("PYTHON")
with open("s.txt") as f:
    f.seek(2)
    x = f.read(3)
    print(n, x, f.tell())
```
questions.explanation_en: write() returns the number of characters written: 6. seek(2) moves the file pointer to offset 2, which is the character T (P=0, Y=1, T=2). read(3) reads THO, and the pointer moves on to offset 5, which tell() reports.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: What is the main advantage of opening a file with with open('a.txt') as f: ?

options.en: The file is opened in both read and write mode together
The whole file is loaded into memory before any reading
The file is closed automatically, even if an error occurs
The file is locked so no other program can open it

questions.explanation_en: with uses the file object as a context manager. When the block ends, normally or because of an exception, the file's close() is called automatically. This avoids leaving files open and losing data that has not been written yet.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("12")
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("34")
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("56")
with open("log.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
```
questions.explanation_en: The first 'w' writes 12. The second 'w' truncates the file, so 12 is lost and the file holds 34. 'a' keeps the contents and adds 56 at the end, giving 3456. The final read prints 3456.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import csv
with open("marks.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["roll", "marks"])
    w.writerow([1, 95])
with open("marks.csv", newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.reader(f))
print(rows[1], len(rows))
```
questions.explanation_en: The file has two lines: roll,marks and 1,95. csv.reader returns each line as a list of strings; it does not convert numbers. So rows[1] is ['1', '95'], and rows has 2 rows, the header included.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en: Which csv.writer method writes every row of a list of lists in a single call?
questions.explanation_en: writerow(row) writes one row, and writerows(rows) writes every row of an iterable of rows. writelines() is a method of ordinary file objects that writes strings without CSV formatting. There is no writeall() method.

questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=['a', 'b', 'c'])
print(s['b'] + s.iloc[2], len(s))
```
questions.explanation_en: A Series is a one-dimensional labelled array. s['b'] picks by label and gives 20; s.iloc[2] picks by position (0-based) and gives 30. 20 + 30 = 50, and the Series has 3 elements.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['A', 'B', 'C'], 'marks': [70, 85, 90]})
print(df.shape, df['marks'].max())
```
questions.explanation_en: Each dictionary key becomes a column and each list holds that column's values. There are 3 rows and 2 columns, so shape is (rows, columns) = (3, 2). df['marks'].max() is 90.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([5, 6, 7, 8], index=[1, 2, 3, 4])
print(s.loc[1:3].sum(), s.iloc[1:3].sum())
```
questions.explanation_en: loc slices by label and includes the end label, so s.loc[1:3] takes labels 1, 2 and 3: 5 + 6 + 7 = 18. iloc slices by position and excludes the end, like a Python list, so s.iloc[1:3] takes positions 1 and 2: 6 + 7 = 13.

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
df1 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [5, 6], 'B': [7, 8]})
print(pd.concat([df1, df2]).shape, pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1).shape)
```
questions.explanation_en: pd.concat() joins along axis 0 by default, stacking the rows: 2 + 2 = 4 rows and the same 2 columns, so (4, 2). With axis=1 the frames are placed side by side: 2 rows and 2 + 2 = 4 columns, so (2, 4).

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
left = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3], 'name': ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Gita']})
right = pd.DataFrame({'id': [2, 3, 4], 'marks': [50, 60, 70]})
m = pd.merge(left, right, on='id')
print(len(m), list(m.columns))
```
questions.explanation_en: pd.merge() joins two DataFrames like a database join, with how='inner' by default. Only id values found in both frames (2 and 3) are kept, so there are 2 rows. The key column id appears once, followed by the other columns: ['id', 'name', 'marks'].

questions.chapter: Programming — Python: Data Types, Collections, File Handling & Pandas
questions.question_en:
What is the output of the following Python code?
```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'roll': [101, 102, 103], 'name': ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Gita']})
df2 = df.set_index('roll')
print(df2.loc[102, 'name'], df2.shape)
```
questions.explanation_en: set_index('roll') returns a new DataFrame whose row labels are the roll values, and roll is no longer a data column. So df2 has 3 rows and 1 column, shape (3, 1). df2.loc[102, 'name'] looks up the row labelled 102: Ravi.

questions.explanation_en: head(n=5) returns the first n rows, and n defaults to 5. tail() returns the last 5 rows in the same way. The column names come from df.columns, and the size from df.shape.

questions.question_en: In pandas, selecting one column of a DataFrame with df['marks'] returns an object of type:
questions.explanation_en: A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labelled table, and each of its columns is a one-dimensional Series that shares the DataFrame's index. df['marks'] returns that Series. df[['marks']], with a list of names, returns a DataFrame.

questions.question_en: In .NET, which component manages memory (garbage collection), security and exception handling while a program runs?
questions.explanation_en: The CLR is the .NET execution engine and sits between the application and the operating system. It loads code, JIT-compiles it, and provides garbage collection, type safety, security and exception handling.

questions.question_en: In .NET, the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler converts:

options.en: C# source code into MSIL code at compile time
MSIL (CIL) code into native machine code at run time
Native machine code back into MSIL code
VB.NET source code into equivalent C# code

questions.explanation_en: .NET language compilers first produce MSIL (CIL), a CPU-independent intermediate code. When a method is first called, the CLR's JIT compiler turns that MSIL into native code for the current CPU.

questions.question_en: The set of basic rules that a .NET language must follow so that its code can be used from other .NET languages is the:
questions.explanation_en: The CLS is a subset of the CTS. It lists the rules that every CLS-compliant language and library must follow (for example, public members should not use unsigned types such as uint). This makes language interoperability possible: a VB.NET program can use a C# library.

questions.question_en: In .NET, C# int and VB.NET Integer both map to System.Int32. Which component defines this common set of types?
questions.explanation_en: The CTS defines how types are declared, used and managed in the runtime, so all .NET languages share one type system. Language keywords such as int (C#) and Integer (VB.NET) are aliases for the same CTS type, System.Int32.

questions.question_en: Code that runs under the control of the CLR, which handles its memory and security, is called:
questions.explanation_en: Managed code is executed by the CLR, which provides garbage collection, type checking and security. Unmanaged code, such as a C++ program compiled straight to machine code, runs directly on the operating system without CLR services.

questions.question_en: In .NET, the Global Assembly Cache (GAC) is used to store:

options.en: Temporary files created by the JIT compiler at run time
Source code files of all installed .NET applications
Objects that the garbage collector has not yet freed
Strong-named assemblies shared by several applications

questions.explanation_en: An assembly (.dll or .exe) is the unit of deployment in .NET and holds MSIL plus a manifest. A private assembly sits in its application's folder. A shared assembly must have a strong name and is installed in the GAC so that many applications can use it.

questions.question_en: Which programming language, designed by Anders Hejlsberg, was released by Microsoft with .NET Framework 1.0 in 2002?
questions.explanation_en: Microsoft released .NET Framework 1.0 in 2002, together with C# 1.0, a language designed by Anders Hejlsberg's team. Java is from Sun Microsystems (now Oracle), Kotlin is from JetBrains and Swift is from Apple.

questions.question_en: Which statement about a static constructor in C# is TRUE?

options.en: It can be overloaded with different parameter lists
It must be called explicitly using the new keyword
It has no parameters and runs once, before the class is first used
It runs again each time a new object is created

questions.explanation_en: A static constructor takes no parameters and no access modifier, and a class can have only one. The CLR calls it automatically, exactly once, before the first instance is created or any static member is used. It is used to initialise static data.

questions.question_en: Which statement about a constructor in C# is TRUE?

options.en: It must always be declared with the return type void
It can be called only once in the whole program
A class is allowed to have only one constructor
It has the same name as its class and no return type

questions.explanation_en: A C# constructor has the same name as the class and no return type, not even void. It runs automatically when an object is created with new. Constructors can be overloaded, and the compiler supplies a default one if none is written.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is a value type in C#?
questions.explanation_en: Value types (int, double, bool, char, enum and struct) hold their data directly, usually on the stack. class, interface, string, arrays and delegates are reference types: the variable holds a reference to an object on the managed heap.

questions.question_en: In C#, the statement object o = 25; converts a value type into a reference type. This conversion is called:
questions.explanation_en: Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap, so it can be treated as System.Object. The reverse, int n = (int)o;, is unboxing and needs an explicit cast.

questions.question_en: In C#, a class member declared internal can be accessed:

options.en: Only in classes derived from it

questions.explanation_en: internal limits access to the current assembly (the same .dll or .exe). private allows only the containing class, protected allows the class and its derived classes, and public allows any code. protected internal combines protected and internal.

questions.question_en: Which C# collection stores key-value pairs with unique keys and compile-time type safety, as a generic replacement for Hashtable?
questions.explanation_en: Hashtable (System.Collections) stores key-value pairs and finds a value by its unique key, but keys and values are just object. Dictionary<TKey, TValue> (System.Collections.Generic) does the same with type safety. List<T> and ArrayList are accessed by index, and Queue<T> is FIFO.

questions.question_en: In VB.NET, which control lets the user select several options from a group at the same time?
questions.explanation_en: Each CheckBox can be ticked or cleared on its own, so any number can be selected. RadioButtons in one group are mutually exclusive, so only one can be selected. A Label shows text and a TextBox takes typed input.

questions.question_en: Which VB.NET control combines a text box with a drop-down list, so the user can pick an item or type a value?
questions.explanation_en: A ComboBox is a text box with a drop-down list. A ListBox shows a list that is always visible and has no editable text area. A CheckBox is a single on/off option, and a PictureBox shows an image.
